candidates.label: et-Tell
candidates.support: Excavated since 1987 and long treated as the leading candidate, with a substantial Roman and Byzantine-period settlement and a possible city gate; critics note the site sits more than a mile from the present shoreline of the Sea of Galilee, awkward for a fishing village.

candidates.label: el-Araj
candidates.support: Systematically excavated since 2016, much closer to the ancient shoreline than et-Tell, with Roman and Byzantine-period layers and a mosaic inscription that excavators argue supports an early Christian association with the site; the debate between the two candidates remains unresolved among specialists.

summary.text: Bethsaida is named in the Gospels as the home town of the apostles Peter, Andrew and Philip and the setting of the feeding of the five thousand and other episodes; its location is disputed between two excavated sites on the northern shore of the Sea of Galilee.

history.text: Ancient sources, including Josephus, describe Bethsaida being refounded and elevated to a Greek-style city named Julias by the tetrarch Philip early in the first century AD, a status that both excavation teams look for evidence of at their respective candidate sites.

Two older candidates, el-Mes'adiye and the Tabgha area, were proposed in earlier twentieth-century surveys but receive little attention in recent scholarly literature, which has focused on the et-Tell/el-Araj debate.

John 12:21 calls Philip's home town 'Bethsaida of Galilee.' Josephus, however, places Bethsaida, which the tetrarch Philip raised to a city named Julias, in Lower Gaulanitis, and gives Galilee's eastern border as the territories of Hippos and Gadara and Gaulanitis. Scholars discuss whether John's wording reflects a wider use of 'Galilee' for the land around the lake or points to a town on the Galilean shore; some have proposed a second Bethsaida there. Both of this record's candidate sites are put forward as Bethsaida-Julias, so for about AD 50 this project places Bethsaida in the Roman province of Judea, which governed Philip's former tetrarchy from AD 44 until AD 53, rather than in the Galilee district.

scripture.textWEB: “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works had been done in Tyre and Sidon which were done in you, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes.
Immediately he made his disciples get into the boat and go ahead to the other side, to Bethsaida, while he himself sent the multitude away.
He came to Bethsaida. They brought a blind man to him and begged him to touch him.
The apostles, when they had returned, told him what things they had done. He took them and withdrew apart to a desert region of a city called Bethsaida.
“Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works had been done in Tyre and Sidon which were done in you, they would have repented long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes.
Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter.
Therefore, these came to Philip, who was from Bethsaida of Galilee, and asked him, saying, “Sir, we want to see Jesus.”
